mcqs.question: Why does autocomplete need a much tighter latency budget than a normal search query?
options: Autocomplete servers are always physically farther from users
It only runs on mobile devices, which have slower networks
It fires on every keystroke rather than once per submitted query, so delays compound visibly
Autocomplete always requires more relevance computation than a full search
mcqs.explanation: A 10-character query triggers 10 lookups instead of one, so even a modest per-request delay becomes visible lag while typing. It isn't about server distance or platform, and autocomplete actually does less computation per request, not more.

mcqs.question: A user has personally searched "catamaran" many times before, but it's a globally rare query. Why might autocomplete still suggest it near the top for that user typing "cat"?
options: The trie always lists rare words before common ones
Personalization signals from the user's own search history can boost a completion above what global frequency alone would suggest
Rare words are always ranked above common words by default
The system ignores frequency entirely and ranks alphabetically
mcqs.explanation: Personalization is one of the blended ranking signals — a user's own history can surface a globally uncommon completion for them specifically. Tries don't inherently rank by rarity, and ranking isn't alphabetical or rarity-first by default.

mcqs.question: A product search box needs suggestions to match anywhere inside a multi-word title, not just its start — searching "shoes" should surface "comfortable blue running shoes." Which approach fits better?
options: A plain trie storing each title as a single string
A hash map keyed by the first letter of each title
Sorting all titles alphabetically and binary-searching
An index-based approach (e.g. edge n-grams in an inverted index) rather than pure prefix-based trie matching
mcqs.explanation: An index-based / search-as-you-type approach is what handles matches anywhere inside a phrase, since a trie only walks matches from the very start of a string. A plain hash map or alphabetical sort don't support this kind of substring completion at all.

mcqs.question: A typeahead feature ranks every matching completion live on each keystroke, and it buckles under load for popular short prefixes. What's the standard fix?
options: Precompute and cache the top-k completions per prefix ahead of time, so the request path is a lookup, not a live computation
Limit users to typing at most 3 characters
Remove the trie and switch to a full table scan
Disable autocomplete for any prefix shorter than 5 characters
mcqs.explanation: Precomputing top-k lists turns an expensive per-keystroke ranking pass into a cheap cache read, which is exactly what a tight latency budget requires. Restricting input length or removing the trie doesn't fix the underlying computation cost.
